common_name: Windy City Ornamental Onion (Large-Flowered Long-Blooming Hybrid Allium)

planting.note: Plant container-grown divisions in spring, or bulbs in fall, in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Windy City is a sterile hybrid bred as a companion to Millenium with larger flower heads on taller stems.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Windy City is a sterile hybrid ornamental onion bred from the same breeding program as the popular Millenium allium, but selected for notably larger rosy-purple globe flowers held on taller, sturdier stems above strap-like, deer- and rabbit-resistant foliage. It blooms from midsummer into early fall, drawing heavy bee and butterfly traffic for weeks, and because it is sterile it does not set seed or self-sow, staying in a tidy, non-spreading clump. Its heat and humidity tolerance make it more reliable in the Gulf South than many ornamental onions, provided drainage is good, and it combines well with coneflowers, black-eyed Susans, and ornamental grasses in a late-summer pollinator planting. Division is needed only occasionally, when clumps become crowded after several years.
sources: Chicago Botanic Garden Plant Evaluation Notes

common_name: Georgia Blue Speedwell (Low Spreading Groundcover Veronica with Vivid Blue Flowers)

planting.note: Plant container-grown divisions in spring or fall in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Georgia Blue spreads by trailing stems that root as they go, quickly forming a low mat useful for edging paths, rock gardens, and small-scale groundcover plantings.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; good drainage is important, as this low groundcover speedwell dislikes standing water. Georgia Blue is a low, mat-forming veronica that spreads via trailing stems, producing a carpet of small bronze-green leaves smothered in early spring by masses of vivid gentian-blue flowers with tiny white eyes, one of the earliest and most eye-catching groundcover blooms of the season. Its dense, semi-evergreen foliage continues to provide low textural groundcover after the spring flower show fades, and light shearing after bloom keeps the mat tidy and can prompt sparse rebloom later in the season. It is well suited to rock gardens, path edges, and the front of borders where a low, spreading, easy-care perennial is needed, and established plantings tolerate both light foot traffic and short dry spells.
sources: Chicago Botanic Garden Plant Evaluation Notes

common_name: Tickled Pink Veronica (Compact Long-Blooming Pink Spike Speedwell)

planting.note: Plant container-grown divisions in spring or fall in well-drained soil in full sun; deadheading spent spikes promptly encourages a strong repeat bloom later in the season.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun, and avoid heavy, poorly drained ground where veronica is prone to crown rot over winter. Tickled Pink is a compact spike speedwell bred for a long season of clear pink flower spikes held upright over neat, dark green foliage, blooming from late spring into summer and again in fall if deadheaded promptly after the first flush. Its tidy, well-branched habit needs no staking and suits the front to middle of a sunny perennial border, where it draws bees and butterflies over an extended bloom period. Established plants are drought-tolerant once rooted and benefit from division every three to four years to maintain vigor and flowering, since older clumps can become woody and bloom less freely at the center.
sources: Chicago Botanic Garden Plant Evaluation Notes

common_name: Purple Emperor Sedum (Dark Purple-Black Foliage Stonecrop with Pink Fall Flowers)

planting.note: Plant container-grown divisions in spring or fall in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; like other upright sedums, Purple Emperor is drought-tolerant once established and rots readily in wet, heavy soil.

directions: Plant in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; rich, moist soil produces floppy, weak growth in upright sedums, so avoid heavy feeding or fertile ground. Purple Emperor is an upright border sedum selected for deep purple-black foliage and stems that hold their dark color through the growing season, topped in late summer and fall by broad, flat clusters of dusky pink flowers that draw butterflies and bees in large numbers just as many other perennials are fading. Its sturdy, self-supporting stems generally resist the flopping that troubles older tall sedum cultivars, and the dark foliage provides strong color contrast against silver, gray, or chartreuse companion plants all season, not just at bloom time. Extremely drought-tolerant once established, it thrives on neglect in a sunny border and needs only occasional division every few years to keep the clump vigorous; spent flower heads can be left standing through winter for structural interest and bird food.
sources: Chicago Botanic Garden Plant Evaluation Notes

common_name: Vertigo Fountain Grass (Dramatic Dark Purple-Black Ornamental Grass)

planting.note: Plant container-grown divisions after the last frost into full sun in fertile, well-drained soil; Vertigo grows as a fast, dramatic annual accent outside its tropical hardiness range and is usually replanted each year or overwintered indoors as a houseplant.

directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, and feed regularly through the season to fuel this grass's exceptionally fast, dramatic growth. Vertigo is a dwarf selection of Napier grass bred for strikingly dark, near-black-purple blades on a tall, upright, fountain-like clump, providing bold vertical color contrast in beds and large containers unmatched by most other purple ornamental grasses. It grows remarkably quickly through a single warm season, often reaching full size within a few months of planting, and the color deepens with more sun exposure and warmth. Outside the warmest zones it is grown as a dramatic annual accent or container specimen and either replaced each spring or, where a bright indoor spot is available, cut back and overwintered as a houseplant to save the clump for the following year.
sources: Proven Winners — Vertigo fountain grass notes
